vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: prompt-guard
Version: 3.6.2

The prompt-guard skill bundle is a comprehensive security library for AI agents, providing over 650 detection patterns for prompt injection, data exfiltration, and tool abuse. It features a multi-layered defense-in-depth architecture including text normalization, multi-encoding decoders (decoder.py), and an enterprise-grade DLP system (output.py) for redacting sensitive credentials. The bundle includes an optional API client (api_client.py) and a distributed threat intelligence client (hivefence.py) that report anonymized threat metadata (hashes) to external endpoints (pg-secure-api.vercel.app and hivefence-api.seojoon-kim.workers.dev). A system audit utility (audit.py) is also provided to check for common security misconfigurations. The code is well-structured, includes extensive regression tests, and demonstrates clear intent to protect agents rather than attack them.

llm.summary: This appears to be a real prompt-security scanner, but it makes default outbound network calls and reports hashed detection metadata despite mixed offline and optional-API claims.

dimensions.detail: For a prompt scanner, local pattern matching and logging are proportionate, but default outbound calls to author-controlled endpoints for remote pattern loading and HiveFence reporting exceed the minimum needed for offline scanning.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: Installation is a standard Python package with a console entry point and no observed install-time script execution, but dependencies use broad minimum constraints rather than pinned reviewed versions.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill text and package comments repeatedly describe offline or optional API behavior, while SKILL.md also says the API is enabled by default and the code confirms default network use; that inconsistency materially affects user expectations.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No backdoor, scheduler, shell persistence, or automatic privilege escalation was found; the package can write local security logs by default and can cache HiveFence data under ~/.clawdbot when that client is used.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

dimensions.detail: The bundled patterns, tests, and examples mostly match the stated purpose of detecting prompt injection, exfiltration, jailbreaks, and DLP issues, but the default PromptGuard constructor fetches remote early/premium regex patterns and HIGH+ detections are reported to HiveFence by default.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

llm.guidance: Review this before installing in privacy-sensitive or offline environments. Disable the API and HiveFence reporting unless you explicitly want remote pattern updates and telemetry, and consider pinning dependencies for production use. The malware-looking strings in the package are mostly detector examples, but the default network behavior is real and should be treated as an opt-in requirement by deployers.
llm.findings:
[YR1] expected: Reverse-shell strings were found in README, changelog, tests, and pattern definitions as examples or regex signatures to detect malicious prompts, not as executed payloads.
[P5] expected: The harmful-content phrase appears in a unit test asserting that encoded harmful text is detected; it is evidence of scanner coverage rather than an instruction to users' agents.
[AE6] expected: Inter-character and hidden-text evasion references are part of documented prompt-injection detection coverage; I did not find those strings used as hidden runtime instructions.
[YR4] expected: Offensive-tool and prompt-injection terms such as webhook.site, burpcollaborator, and ignore-previous-instructions appear as detection examples or patterns, which is coherent for this security scanner.
[SC2] expected: The curl-pipe-to-shell text is documented as an attack example to block, not an install or runtime command issued by the skill.
[PE3] expected: Credential-path strings such as .env and credentials.json are used in DLP and exfiltration-detection patterns, not as code paths that read local secrets.
[AR3] expected: Anti-refusal and override-safety phrases are presented as malicious prompt examples the scanner should flag.
[P1] expected: Instruction-override phrases are detection examples and pattern inputs, not active instructions to the evaluating agent.
[T09] unexpected: The A.I.G telemetry finding is supported: logging_utils.report_to_hivefence defaults enabled and auto_report to true, and engine.analyze calls it for HIGH+ detections, sending a deterministic message hash plus category, severity, and client metadata to an external endpoint.
[T08] unexpected: The A.I.G remote-pattern finding is supported: engine.py enables the API by default, uses a built-in beta key, fetches early/premium regex patterns on construction, and trusts a checksum delivered by the same remote service.
[T08] unexpected: The dependency finding is a hardening concern rather than evidence of compromise: pyproject.toml uses broad minimum dependency constraints and no lockfile or hashes.
